claims.text: The starting coating has a mixed FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
The starting coating has coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries primarily govern the coating's creep resistance.
Coherent interphase boundaries impede dislocation motion.
Coherent interphase boundaries slow localized atomic diffusion.
Impeded dislocation motion and slower localized diffusion delay plastic deformation under sustained stress.
A controlled thermal treatment can disrupt FCC/BCC boundary coherence without changing the overall phase composition.
Disrupting boundary coherence reduces the boundaries' barrier effect.
Reduced boundary coherence increases dislocation mobility.
Thermally treated samples with disrupted boundary coherence will have a higher creep strain rate than the intact-boundary baseline under identical loading conditions.
Thermally treated samples with disrupted boundary coherence will show an earlier onset of plastic deformation than the intact-boundary baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies at moderate temperatures where grain-boundary sliding, phase transformations, and other secondary creep mechanisms do not dominate.
The quantitative effect depends on the degree of boundary disruption and contributions from other microstructural features.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate increase or a marked dislocation-behavior difference after verified boundary disruption would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
